This shares the same "in" counter used by mint/repay paths, but liquidation consumes value from the journal's `accAmountIn` allowance while incrementing `inPerChain`. Because `inPerChain` is used to track both consumed journal allowance for mint/repay (which credit the user) and consumed liquidation allowance, an attacker with a legitimate journal can first call `mintExternal` to bump `inPerChain` and then cannot liquidate, or conversely the semantics mix. Also `liquidateAmount` is directly credited to `inPerChain` even though the debt repaid may be less than `liquidateAmount` (repaid amount depends on `actualRepayAmount` inside `__repay`), so `inPerChain` for the source chain is decoupled from actual value delivered.
hypotheses.attackPath: A holder of a large journal calls `liquidateExternal` where `liquidateAmount` is sized to consume `_accAmountIn`, while `__liquidate` internally repays only the borrower's actual outstanding debt (smaller). The `inPerChain[_sender]` counter increases by the full `liquidateAmount` even though the L1-observed amount corresponding to the repay was smaller, wasting the proof allowance and misrecording value.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent `inPerChain` accounting allows some users to consume more/less of the proof allowance than their real on-chain activity, permitting griefing of other users of the same sender or double usage of the same proof.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `actualRepayAmount` returned by `__liquidate`/`_liquidate` for the `inPerChain` accounting, not the input `liquidateAmount`; keep separate counters per operation type.

hypotheses.title: Operator.checkOutflowVolumeLimit trusts calling mToken to send its own address; any listed market can drain limit and block others
hypotheses.description: `checkOutflowVolumeLimit` accepts `msg.sender` if `markets[msg.sender].isListed` and, when `limitPerTimePeriod > 0`, accumulates `cumulativeOutflowVolume += amountInUSD`. Since the limit is per-Operator across all markets, a single market (or an attacker who can cause big outflows in a single market) can fill the aggregate limit, denying other markets' exit operations. Additionally `resetOutflowVolume` requires `onlyOwner`, but the automatic reset only occurs when `block.timestamp > lastOutflowResetTimestamp + outflowResetTimeWindow` *and* the function is invoked. If `limitPerTimePeriod` is changed, `cumulativeOutflowVolume` is not reset (only on automatic reset or explicit owner call), so a prior window's volume carries over. The front-runability comes from any listed market caller.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user triggers a large redeem/mintExternal/performExtensionCall in one market to max `cumulativeOutflowVolume`; other users in other markets then cannot redeem/borrow until the time window resets.
hypotheses.impact: Core functions (`redeem`, `performExtensionCall`) revert with `Operator_OutflowVolumeReached()` for the remainder of the window — denial of withdrawals/collateral exits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track outflow per market, or reset `cumulativeOutflowVolume` when `limitPerTimePeriod` is updated; consider a per-user cap.

hypotheses.title: Rebalancer sends msg.value to bridge but saveEth/save can steal accumulated ETH and bridge receives arbitrary value
hypotheses.description: `sendMsg` is callable by any `REBALANCER_EOA` and forwards `msg.value` to an arbitrary whitelisted bridge while calling `extractForRebalancing` on an allow-listed `_market` to pull `_amount` underlying, approved to the bridge. The bridge `sendMsg` signatures take `_message`/`bridgeData` supplied by the caller; `EverclearBridge.sendMsg` returns left-over `_extractedAmount - params.amount` to `_market`, but `AccrossBridge.sendMsg` and others trust the encoded amounts. Nothing ties the message amounts to `_amount` beyond a per-bridge check, and the whitelist allows the rebalancer EOA to pick any bridge. A misconfigured/compromised-but-whitelisted bridge or a crafted `_message` can route funds to attacker-controlled destinations.
hypotheses.attackPath: A compromised REBALANCER_EOA (or a role held by an attacker via misconfiguration) calls `sendMsg` with a whitelisted but malicious bridge, `_amount` pulled from the market, and a message directing funds elsewhere.
hypotheses.impact: Market underlying is extracted and routed away, causing loss of market funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate message fields (input asset, amount, destination) against `_msg.dstChainId`/`_msg.token` inside `Rebalancer` before extraction, and restrict the bridge/destination matrix rather than verifying only that the bridge is whitelisted.

hypotheses.title: Rebalancer has no nonce/expiry on sendMsg and allows replay of the same Msg across transactions
hypotheses.description: `sendMsg` accepts `Msg calldata _msg` (`dstChainId`, `token`, `message`, `bridgeData`), stores it under an incrementing `nonce`, and calls the bridge. There is no per-user signature check or replay protection tying a message to a specific nonce: the same `_msg` payload can be submitted repeatedly by any REBALANCER_EOA and will trigger repeated `extractForRebalancing` calls and bridge sends, each moving fresh tokens. The `logs[dstChainId][nonce]` map is informational only. The `allowedList[_market]` check is applied after credits/debits are computed for `currentTransferSize`, but the actual token movement is delegated to `extractForRebalancing` (on mToken) and then to the bridge.
hypotheses.attackPath: A REBALANCER_EOA submits the same `Msg` with `_bridge`, `_market`, `_amount` multiple times; each call extracts `_amount` from the market and sends via bridge. Because the min/max window logic allows repeated submissions, the total sent can exceed desired single-transfer intent if the cap is high or 0.
hypotheses.impact: Repeated extraction of market funds to a bridge, potentially draining the market if the account controlling REBALANCER_EOA is compromised, with no per-message nonce to prevent unintended duplicate sends.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a non-unique message nonce (per chain/token) in `Msg` and require the stored nonce to match; require caller to pass an expected nonce and revert on reuse.

hypotheses.title: Repay charged against outflow limit using full repayAmount even though only actualRepayAmount burns
hypotheses.description: `repayExternal` calls `_checkOutflow(CommonLib.computeSum(repayAmount))` before decoding journals, so the outflow volume counter is incremented by the requested `repayAmount`. Inside `_repayExternal` the actual deduction is `actualRepayAmount = _repayBehalf(...)`, which can differ (e.g. capped at debt) and is only checked `<= _accAmountIn - acc[].inPerChain[_sender]`. So the global USD outflow counter is increased by more (or by a different amount) than the actual consumption, while `performExtensionCall` for withdraw/borrow also relies on the same `limitPerTimePeriod`.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user submits `repayExternal` with `repayAmount` values summing close to the period limit but with debts much smaller than that. `_checkOutflow` bumps `cumulativeOutflowVolume` by the requested total, or conversely a repaid amount less than requested remains counted, permanently distorting the global outflow volume.
hypotheses.impact: The global outflow limiter (`cumulativeOutflowVolume` vs `limitPerTimePeriod`), which protects the protocol from draining, is inflated/mis-charged by repay flows, allowing the limit to be consumed or bypassed incorrectly and affecting other users' ability to withdraw/borrow up to the intended cap.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the actual repaid amounts and call `_checkOutflow` with the sum actually consumed (post `_repayBehalf`), or reconcile the outflow counter to the actual `actualRepayAmount` inside the loop.

hypotheses.title: processExtensionCall outflow check bypasses acc.outPerChain accounting and reuses mint SUM limit
hypotheses.description: `performExtensionCall` calls `_checkOutflow(amount)` using `amount` and only afterwards does `_redeem`/`_borrow` with `doTransfer = false`, then adds `acc[dstChainId].outPerChain[msg.sender] += _amount` (note `_amount` is set only in the redeem branch; for `actionType == 2` `_amount` remains `amount`). The outflow limit `limitPerTimePeriod` is meant per time window but `operator.checkOutflowVolumeLimit` uses `markets[msg.sender].isListed`, which is the mToken being called; since `extractForRebalancing` and `performExtensionCall` both add to `cumulativeOutflowVolume`, a user can chain `mintExternal`-style flows that only increment `inPerChain` while using the same limit accounting. Also `_checkOutflow` is called before `_borrow` validates liquidity, and the emitted event for borrow uses `_amount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user calls `performExtensionCall(2, amount, dstChainId)` repeatedly across allowed chains. Because `acc[dstChainId].outPerChain` is tracked but not bounded by any per-chain outflow, and the `_borrow` path accrues the user's borrow but doesn't receive funds locally (doTransfer false), it increments out accounting without sending value while `_checkOutflow` records the amount against a shared global limit.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent out/in accounting lets a user's off-chain liability (`outPerChain`) diverge from the global outflow bound; can be used to exhaust/confuse the shared `limitPerTimePeriod` and produce negative net positions on extension chains reflecting incorrectly in later proofs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure `_checkOutflow` and `acc[].outPerChain` track exactly the amounts moved per chain and validate `actionType`-specific constraints (e.g. borrow liquidity check before out accounting).

hypotheses.title: mErc20Host _repayExternal charges outflow before validating journals and repays against wrong sender
hypotheses.description: `_checkOutflow(CommonLib.computeSum(repayAmount))` is charged up front against `msg.sender`'s cumulative outflow budget, before journals are validated and before the corresponding `_accAmountIn` for each `_sender` is checked. An attacker who is a batch proof forwarder can submit arbitrary `repayAmount[]` values to drain a victim's outflow budget (limitPerTimePeriod) without ever paying anything: the pre-check succeeds and the journals' userToValidate `_checkProofCall` will revert; but a malicious batch where sum matches real outflow budget doesn't make sense since it reverts. The actionable class: `computeSum` uses caller-supplied `repayAmount`, not `actualRepayAmount`, and outflow is consumed by `actualRepayAmount`, which can be lower (fee-on-transfer tokens). Result: cumulative outflow can diverge from actual outflow used.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker submits `repayExternal` with amounts summing to the outflow limit; the outflow check runs and increments `cumulativeOutflowVolume` via `checkOutflowVolumeLimit` on `CommonLib.computeSum(repayAmount)` before the actual repay. 2) If the validation later reverts, whole tx reverts — not exploitable. 3) But `__repay` internal uses `repayAmountFinal` which can be less than requested with `doTransfer=false` for fee tokens; outflow is then charged for the full `repayAmount` while only `actualRepayAmount` is debited (outflow is over-charged) — a DoS vector for honest users during normal fee-token use.
hypotheses.impact: Outflow volume accounting is skewed by inflated charges for `doTransfer=false` calls, consuming the `limitPerTimePeriod` and blocking legitimate user operations; end-users who use fee-on-transfer tokens can't migrate.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `_checkOutflow` after the loop with the actual measured outflow, or share the check outcome with the actual transferred amount.

hypotheses.title: claimMalda allows any caller to claim rewards on behalf of any holder
hypotheses.severity: Low/Medium (reportable as Medium below threshold note)
hypotheses.description: All three `claimMalda` overloads accept arbitrary `holder`/`holders` with no check that `msg.sender` is the holder or approved. `_claim` calls `_distributeSupplierMalda`/`_distributeBorrowerMalda` and then `IRewardDistributor(rewardDistributor).claim(holders)`, which transfers accumulated reward tokens to each holder. While the funds go to the holder, the caller controls timing and can force-distribute and claim on behalf of others.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any address calls `claimMalda(victim)`; `_claim` updates the victim's reward indices and then `RewardDistributor._claim` transfers their accrued rewards to the victim. There is no loss of funds to attacker, but the function name and interface imply only holders can trigger their own claim; a caller can trigger distribution/claim state changes on any account at arbitrary times.
hypotheses.impact: No direct theft; griefing/DoS is limited because `_grantReward` silently returns `amount` if the distributor lacks balance, so the call still succeeds. The behavior breaks the implicit access control of claim functions and can be abused to force reward transfer or to consume the distributor balance on behalf of other accounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `holders[j] == msg.sender` (or an explicit approval mechanism) in the public claim entry points, or document that claiming is intentionally permissionless and remove the holder parameter for the user-facing path.

hypotheses.title: withdrawGasFees sends full ETH balance regardless of gasHelper minimum, denies refund to other users
hypotheses.description: `withdrawGasFees` transfers `address(this).balance` to a caller-specified `receiver`, gated only by `_getSequencerRole()`. Since the contract accepts ETH via `payable performExtensionCall` and its gas requirement is `msg.value >= gasHelper.gasFees(dstChainId)`, this function gives role holders the entire retained balance. It does not conflict with attacker capability, but it strips ETH needed to refund or reimburse gas, and if any cross-chain refund path relies on contract ETH, this can drain it.
hypotheses.attackPath: A sequencer-role holder calls `withdrawGasFees(receiver)` with their own address and sweeps all unpaid gas.
hypotheses.impact: Any user who overpaid gas in `performExtensionCall` can never recover it once the sequencer sweeps.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `withdrawGasFees` to surplus ETH not attributable to pending refunds, or document that sequencer collects overpaid gas and remove `msg.value < required` refund expectations.

hypotheses.title: RewardDistributor._grantReward reads balanceOf on token == rewardToken meaning MALDA reward token must be an mToken
hypotheses.description: `_grantReward` computes `remaining = ImToken(token).balanceOf(address(this))` and calls `ImToken(token).transfer(user, amount)`, casting the reward token to `ImToken`. Rewards should presumably be a normal ERC-20 (MALDA), but `ImToken` is the mToken interface, whose `transfer` returns bool, which happens to match ERC-20. So this works only if the reward token has a compatible interface. If the MALDA token is a standard ERC-20 it still complies. But `_grantReward` is also called from `grantReward` and `_claim` — if a reward token reverts on transfer or returns no data (USDT-like), `ImToken.transfer` ABI decoding returns bool that may be misinterpreted.
hypotheses.attackPath: If a whitelisted reward token doesn't return bool (e.g., USDT), `_grantReward` reverts on ABI decode, and `claim` reverts for every holder because `rewardTokens` iterates all tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Claim DoS for all users, and any contract-call reward token unsupported by `ImToken` interface breaks claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20` for reward transfers and drop the `ImToken` cast; alternatively restrict reward tokens to a known ERC-20 type.
